turns.en: My co-founder Andrew Blevens and I were at Recursion looking at a small molecule on a screen, and then a medicinal chemist walked by us, this name Mike Karesi, and Mike was like, hey, looks like a Stuart Tribert molecule. And then we were like, oh no, you can tell just by walking by and be like who made this? That's horrifying. And if the models can identify the chemist by looking at the molecule alone, then maybe the models can infer chemist intent, which means maybe they don't learn anything at all.
turns.zh: 我和我的联合创始人 Andrew Blevens 在 Recursion 时，正看着屏幕上的一个小分子，然后一位药物化学家走过，名叫 Mike Karesi，Mike 说，嘿，看起来像 Stuart Tribert 的分子。然后我们想，哦不，你光走过去就能看出这是谁做的？太可怕了。如果模型仅通过观察分子就能识别化学家，那么也许模型能推断化学家的意图，这意味着也许它们什么都没学到。

turns.en: Well, they did learn something, yeah, they don't learn physics.
turns.zh: 嗯，它们确实学到了一些东西，是的，它们不学物理。

turns.en: We downloaded all chemicals from all chemists at Kemble, which is the biggest repository of these things and their activities. Every chemist who published more than, I think it was 30 papers and 600 molecules. So you get all the molecules and all the stuff. It's 1,815 chemists. And then we trained a classifier to predict a chemist from looking at the molecule alone. And we got a top five accuracy of 60%. We chose to represent the molecules not with any chemical structures or formulas at all, but just a vector of the probability of creator. So now it's this 1,800 element vector and it's got some probability of who made it. And you can use that representation and then train a model to predict activity from Kemble and it does as well as if you use chemical formulas. We really think that it's learning a lot of sociology. It's not learning ground truth. When you train models on the exhaust, you might be in trouble.
turns.zh: 我们从 Kemble 下载了所有化学家的所有化学品，这是这些及其活性的最大存储库。每个发表超过，我想是 30 篇论文和 600 个分子的化学家。所以你得到了所有分子和所有东西。有 1,815 位化学家。然后我们训练了一个分类器，仅通过观察分子来预测化学家。我们得到了前五准确率 60%。我们选择不用任何化学结构或公式来表示分子，而只是一个创造者概率的向量。所以现在它是一个 1,800 维的向量，有某个人制造它的概率。你可以使用这个表示，然后训练一个模型来预测 Kemble 的活性，它的表现和使用化学公式一样好。我们真的认为它学到了很多社会学。它没有学到 ground truth。当你在尾气上训练模型时，你可能会遇到麻烦。

turns.zh: 欢迎来到 Laten Space AI for Science 播客。我是 R.J. Haniki，Mirror OMIX 的首席技术官，和我一起的是我的联合主持人 Brandon Anderson。他在 Ato atomic AI 开发 RNA 疗法。

turns.zh: 非常兴奋今天能请到 Ian Quigley 来到演播室。今天，这一集将会很精彩。非常激动。嗯，Ian 是 Leash Bio 的联合创始人兼 CEO。呃，在我看来，这是过去几年我最喜欢的年轻科技生物公司之一。你知道，在高层次上，嗯，Leash 结合了认知严谨性、疯狂规模的数据收集，并且，呃，对开放科学有坚定的承诺，还有一系列令人难以置信的博客文章，我们今天会涵盖很多，但我认为这些文章真正告诉你如何在非常困难的领域以正确的方式做机器学习。我想我会有些有趣的轶事，希望能在这一集中穿插。但是，是的，首先，呃，感谢你来到这里，呃，你知道，你的，呃，在我们开始之前，你有什么关于我们想告诉我们的吗？

turns.en: Um no thanks that was very kind. Yeah we uh we founded Leash uh historically um after being confronted by a particular problem of trying to predict small molecules binding to protein targets uh and then finding that the data that was out there was kind of wanting and so we went out and built this thing at a reasonable scale to kind of try to go after it.
turns.zh: 嗯，不，谢谢，你太客气了。是的，我们，呃，我们创立 Leash 的历史上，嗯，是在遇到一个特定问题之后，即试图预测小分子与蛋白质靶点的结合，呃，然后发现现有的数据有些不足，所以我们出去以合理的规模构建了这个东西，试图去攻克它。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah. So reasonable scale. Um, you're founded upon the idea of doing something called a DNA encoded library. Every person I've ever met who has touched a Dell has come out severely traumatized. I I don't know any person who has ever said Dells. That's a great idea. Let's do hundreds or thousands of these things. So why what? And also please explain what a Dell is before you get started.
turns.zh: 是的。所以合理的规模。嗯，你们的创立基于做一种叫做 DNA 编码库的东西。我见过的每一个接触过 DEL 的人出来都严重受创。我不认识任何人说过 DEL。那是个好主意。让我们做数百或数千个这样的东西。所以为什么？而且在你开始之前，请解释一下什么是 DEL。

turns.en: Yes. Yes. Uh so when you're going after a small molecule drug discovery, uh the ultimate goal is to get a small molecule or a dinky chemical to bind to the protein that you think is causing the problem in a disease. Uh and then go from there. Uh and some of these proteins are pretty easy to find chemical material that sticks to you and some are harder. One way to go about this is to have a lot of different chemicals in different tubes. Uh and you then dunk the protein in one tube at a time and it kind of takes forever. Uh, and then a different solution that was proposed uh, some years ago now was maybe if you had a lot of chemicals in the tube at once and then one tube and then you've got a small DNA barcode that's physically attached to each small molecule. You dunk your protein in the tube kind of like a fish hook. You pull out different ones that bind uh, and then you sequence the DNA of those. And so the idea is that you could then pull this large number of molecules and then you wouldn't have the logistical overhead of trying to go across large numbers of tubes or individual wells and plates. And so what's happened downstream of that is that you've got chemical libraries that if you do one tube at a time, the biggest ones in the world are in the low single-digit millions. With Dell's, the largest one that has been produced um is 40 trillion molecules. Um there's some problems when they get that big, but that is the kind of scale that you could try to attempt with this technology. So the way you create these things is you you uh use this combinatorial chemistry where you have these building blocks and then you you build the library piece by piece but you build it combinatorilially. So
turns.zh: 是的。是的。呃，所以当你进行小分子药物发现时，呃，最终目标是让一个小分子或微小的化学物质结合到你认为在疾病中引起问题的蛋白质上。呃，然后从那里开始。呃，其中一些蛋白质很容易找到粘附的化学物质，有些则更难。一种方法是把许多不同的化学物质放在不同的管子里。呃，然后你一次将蛋白质浸入一个管子中，这几乎要花很长时间。呃，然后几年前提出的另一种解决方案是，也许如果你把很多化学物质放在一个管子里，然后每个小分子都物理连接一个小 DNA 条形码。你像鱼钩一样将蛋白质浸入管中。你拉出结合的不同分子，呃，然后对这些分子的 DNA 进行测序。所以这个想法是，你可以拉出大量分子，然后你就不必承担跨越大量试管或单个孔和板的物流开销。所以下游发生的事情是，你有化学库，如果一次一个管子，世界上最大的在低个位数百万。使用 DEL，已经产生的最大的是 40 万亿个分子。呃，当它们变得那么大时会有一些问题，但这是你可以尝试用这种技术达到的规模。所以你创建这些东西的方式是，你使用组合化学，你有这些构建块，然后你一块一块地构建库，但你是组合地构建它。所以

turns.en: That is correct. Yes. Yes. And so to unpack that a little bit uh if you've got you know some number of millions of molecules what this really means is it is a combinatorial mixture of building blocks and the number of building blocks is going to be a lot smaller than the final product of all of those. So you might be squared or cubed, right? Uh in some different uh example. So it's not uncommon for there to be maybe thousands or tens of thousands of building blocks that would then generate a chemical library of many millions of molecules. And this is restrictive in some ways because you know you're stuck with a smaller number of building blocks. But one thing that's really nice about it for machine learning is that you've got all these different combinations of things that look very similar to each other except for maybe one or two changes. And so that, you know, I'm sure going to get into this later, uh, but that does really enable comparisons so that you can identify, oh, it's this part of the small molecule that's driving the binding because I see a lot of variations in this other part that's not affecting the behavior too much. Uh, and that turns out to be incredibly useful.
turns.zh: 没错。是的。是的。所以稍微解释一下，呃，如果你有数百万个分子，这实际上意味着它是构建块的组合混合物，构建块的数量会比所有最终产物小得多。所以可能是平方或立方，对吧？呃，在一些不同的例子中。所以有数千或数万个构建块，然后生成数百万个分子的化学库并不罕见。这在某些方面是限制性的，因为你知道你被困在较少数量的构建块中。但对机器学习来说，一个非常好的事情是，你有所有这些不同的组合，它们看起来非常相似，除了可能有一两处变化。所以，你知道，我肯定稍后会谈到这个，呃，但这确实使得比较成为可能，这样你可以识别，哦，是小分子的这一部分驱动了结合，因为我看到另一部分有很多变化，但没有太大影响行为。呃，这被证明是非常有用的。

turns.en: The other aspect of this is how you do the readout, which is this DNA sequencing. This has been a big theme on the podcast. We've had many uh guests who have had some variation of we do something crazy and then we convert the reading into a DNA sequencing uh readout. So how does this work and uh why is this so useful?
turns.zh: 另一个方面是你如何进行读出，即 DNA 测序。这在本播客中一直是一个大主题。我们有很多嘉宾，他们都有某种变体，我们做一些疯狂的事情，然后我们将读数转换为 DNA 测序读出。那么这是如何工作的，呃，为什么这么有用？

turns.en: Right. Yeah. I would definitely say that it is a party line at leash that if you're going to go off and try to do uh life science stuff uh and couple it with machine learning approaches. There's really only really only one scalable technology in town and that technology is taking pictures. Sequencing DNA is another way of taking pictures. Uh and so it's basically pictures and DNA sequencing.
turns.zh: 对。是的。我绝对会说，在 Leash 有一条路线，如果你要去做生命科学的东西，呃，并将其与机器学习方法结合起来。真的只有一个可扩展的技术，那就是拍照。测序 DNA 是另一种拍照方式。呃，所以基本上就是拍照和 DNA 测序。

turns.en: And if you can shovel your challenging problem into that using one of those approaches as a readout. So for you know like Recursion takes actual pictures of cells and a bunch of other groups do that, like INRIA does that, and then almost everyone else with the spatial mix stuff or other approaches, they'll do some mixture of pictures and sequencing, which is also pictures. Yeah, there'll be some proteomics people out there who are going to disagree with me, but I'd still argue the scale is not there yet.
turns.zh: 如果你能把你的难题塞进那套流程，用其中一种方法作为读出手段。比如 Recursion 直接拍细胞的照片，还有一堆其他团队也这么做，像 INRIA 就这么干；然后几乎其他所有人用空间混合那套或者别的路子，他们会把拍照和测序混着来，而测序其实也是拍照。对，肯定有些蛋白质组学的人会不同意我，但我还是认为规模还没到。

turns.en: Hot take number one.
turns.zh: 第一个劲爆观点。

turns.en: Yeah. And one of the really cool things about sequencing is that it is dirt cheap. You can, you know, extremely scalable, very well-established technique, like we're very good at it.
turns.zh: 对。测序最酷的一点就是它便宜得离谱。它极度可扩展，是非常成熟的技术，我们非常擅长它。

turns.en: It is very, very cheap. It is getting cheaper all the time. There was a little while where it kind of plateaued in terms of the price dropping, but now a bunch of new companies have started up and they're driving it down again.
turns.zh: 它确实非常非常便宜，而且一直在变便宜。有一小段时间价格下降有点停滞，但现在一堆新公司冒出来，又把价格压下去了。

turns.en: And so we very much look at the trajectory of sequencing cost dropping, and it has implications for how we think about data collection and the scale that we're doing. Yeah, it's really nice.
turns.zh: 所以我们非常关注测序成本下降的轨迹，这会影响我们如何看待数据采集以及我们做的规模。对，这真的很好。

turns.en: That's cool. So you have these components that you are mixing together to form this combinatorial mixture of molecules, and each of those components is barcoded. Is that right?
turns.zh: 这很酷。所以你有这些组件，把它们混在一起形成这种组合式的分子混合物，而每个组件都带条形码。是这样吗？

turns.en: That's correct. And so then they kind of bind together because they're these protein chains or these amino acid chains that will click onto the ends of each other and fold together, and then they either bind or don't bind to your target.
turns.zh: 没错。然后它们会彼此结合，因为它们是这些蛋白链或氨基酸链，会咔嗒一下接到彼此的末端并折叠在一起，然后它们要么结合你的靶标，要么不结合。

turns.en: So first of all, how do you know that they bound to your target?
turns.zh: 那么首先，你怎么知道它们结合到了你的靶标上？

turns.en: Yeah. So first of all, it is very much like this sort of fish hook analogy, where if you were to — so right now the target is some protein or a protein complex that you're going to try to find chemical material to bind to. It's attached to a solid support. And so some folks do it a variety of different ways, but the way that we usually do it is it's attached to a magnetic bead. And so you dunk this bead in this complex mixture of all these small molecules. And in a very easy case, let's pretend that the protein has a very distinctively shaped hole in it. You dunk it in there, and then the chemicals in that pool, some tiny fraction of them, have the appropriate shape and electronics that they're going to bind into this very distinctly shaped hole. Then you pull this protein back out, and you only pull out the things that are in that hole. You rinse it a couple times in some way. And then you sequence the DNA of those things that come out that are in that hole.
turns.zh: 对。首先，这非常像鱼钩的类比：现在靶标是某个蛋白或蛋白复合物，你要试着找到能与之结合的化学物质。它被固定在一个固相载体上。有人用各种不同的方式，但我们通常的做法是把它固定在一颗磁珠上。然后你把这颗珠子浸到所有这些小分子组成的复杂混合物里。在最简单的情况下，假设这个蛋白上有一个形状非常独特的洞。你把它浸进去，然后那个池子里的化学物质中，有一小部分具有合适的形状和电子特性，能结合进这个形状独特的洞里。然后你把这个蛋白拉出来，你只拉出那些在洞里的东西。你再用某种方式冲洗几次。然后你对那些出来、在洞里的东西的 DNA 进行测序。

turns.en: Okay? And then when you say sequence the DNA, you're basically amplifying the barcodes that are in there.
turns.zh: 好？然后你说对 DNA 测序，你基本上就是在扩增里面的条形码。

turns.en: That's correct. And so then you can — so amplify meaning PCR or something like that.
turns.zh: 没错。然后你就可以——扩增指的是 PCR 之类的。

turns.en: You do a little bit of PCR and then, yeah, then you toss it into the sequencer.
turns.zh: 你做一点 PCR，然后对，然后把它丢进测序仪。

turns.en: And then one thing that you're probably thinking right now is, okay, well, we need to compare it to something to get a good measure of relative enrichment. And so you do have to engineer a bunch of good negative controls to say, oh, well, if I just stuck the bead in there by itself, or are there pan-protein stickiness signals that are going to pull out certain chemical libraries, chemicals from the library? And so you got to think pretty hard about all those things and make a reasonable comparison to the thing you're actually trying to get binders for.
turns.zh: 然后你现在可能在想的一件事是：好，我们需要拿它跟某个东西比较，才能很好地衡量相对富集。所以你确实得设计一堆好的阴性对照，来说：哦，如果我只把珠子单独放进去，或者有没有泛蛋白黏附信号会把某些化学库里的化学物质拉出来？所以你得非常认真地思考所有这些，并跟你真正想找到结合物的那个东西做合理的比较。

turns.en: For the things that bind, you sort of have these combinations of barcodes that all sort of — okay, if this one bound, then I have like these — how many barcodes are we talking about for one protein?
turns.zh: 对于那些结合的，你就有这些条形码的组合，它们都——好，如果这个结合了，那我就有这些——一个蛋白我们说的是多少个条形码？

turns.en: Great question. One small —
turns.zh: 好问题。一个小——

turns.en: For one small molecule.
turns.zh: 对一个小分子。

turns.en: So there's a couple things. One thing, if we want to get into the kind of PCR-based weeds — and so for the audience here, if you're making lots and lots of copies of DNA, there's little subtle biases in the DNA that might make them amplify faster than others. And so you want to control for that. So you put in a little bit of unique sequence in there. So when you have lots of copies, you can then collapse it so that they all came from this one — you know, it's very much just from this one event. And then there's a bunch of other things about barcodes that we worry about at length, which is that when you are trying to stick proteins in there, some of those proteins are going to stick to DNA because that's their job, right? There's lots of proteins whose job it is to interact with the genome in cells and turn things on or turn things off or affect them in some other way, and then you've got this assay where you've got a ton of DNA and you're throwing them in there.
turns.zh: 有几件事。第一，如果我们想深入 PCR 的那些细节——对在座的听众说，如果你在制造大量 DNA 拷贝，DNA 里会有一些细微的偏好，可能让某些拷贝比其他扩增得更快。所以你要控制这一点。你放一点独特的序列进去。这样当你有很多拷贝时，你可以把它们合并，让它们都来自这一个——你知道，就只来自这一个事件。然后还有一堆关于条形码的其他问题，我们很在意，就是当你试着把蛋白放进去时，有些蛋白会黏到 DNA 上，因为那是它们的工作，对吧？有很多蛋白的工作就是与细胞里的基因组相互作用，把东西打开或关掉，或以其他方式影响它们，然后你有了这个实验，里面有大量的 DNA，你把它们扔进去。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And so that can be risky.
turns.zh: 所以那可能有风险。

turns.en: And that can cause false positives, right?
turns.zh: 那会导致假阳性，对吧？

turns.en: Very much so. A lot of people complain about this. This is kind of to the earlier comment about folks having Dell nightmares. This is one of those problems. There's a variety of ways to address it. One thing that we do is we have large numbers of barcodes that each encode one particular type of small molecule. You say here's one small molecule. That's great. Now we have 32 or 48 different barcodes all encoding this one small molecule.
turns.zh: 非常是。很多人抱怨这个。这有点像之前说的有人做 Dell 噩梦。这就是那些问题之一。有各种方法解决它。我们做的一件事是，我们有大量条形码，每个都编码一种特定类型的小分子。你说这是一个小分子。很好。现在我们用 32 或 48 个不同的条形码都编码这一个小分子。

turns.en: Oh, I see.
turns.zh: 哦，我明白了。

turns.en: Right. And so then you know — so like there'll be a single example, one single molecule has got this barcode, and then its neighbor, which is the same chemical formula, will have a different barcode, and then so on for —
turns.zh: 对。然后你知道——比如会有单个例子，一个单分子有这个条形码，然后它的邻居，化学式相同，会有不同的条形码，然后以此类推——

turns.en: So if there's differential there, then you know that you're binding to the DNA instead of the —
turns.zh: 所以如果那里有差异，那你就知道你是结合到了 DNA 上，而不是——

turns.en: That's right. And so for the DNA-protein aficionados in the audience, one really nice thing about this is that because there's DNA in there, you can see if there's a single DNA-encoding barcode that binds way better than everything else, even though it's all the same small molecule, and then you can look at the sequence that you have enriched there, and you can recover the described DNA binding preferences of those proteins.
turns.zh: 没错。所以对在座的 DNA-蛋白爱好者来说，一个非常好的地方是，因为那里有 DNA，你可以看到是否有某个单一的 DNA 编码条形码结合得比所有其他都好，尽管它们都是同一个小分子，然后你可以看你在那里富集到的序列，你就能还原出那些蛋白已知的 DNA 结合偏好。

turns.en: It's like, oh, here's a transcription factor, it binds this series of nucleotides that is very well described, you know, it's like six or eight of them, and then you look at the — you recover the DNA sequences back from this experiment, it's like, oh great, we found the consensus binding motif.
turns.zh: 就像，哦，这是一个转录因子，它结合这一系列核苷酸，这是描述得很清楚的，你知道，大概六到八个，然后你看——你从这个实验里还原出 DNA 序列，就像，哦太好了，我们找到了共有结合基序。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: So I think our protein probably got made right.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得我们的蛋白大概做对了。

turns.en: You have this barcode that you've identified and you've kind of gotten rid of the false positives using the technique that you just said.
turns.zh: 你有了这个你识别出的条形码，而且你用刚才说的技术差不多去掉了假阳性。

turns.en: But one thing I do want to say is that um when DELs were invented uh it was definitely at a time when sequencing was kind of more expensive and it really felt like taking doing sequencing experiments was kind of like a big logistical and financial swing. Um and then when you built the technology at the time and then pointed it at the problems that it was pointed at, it was very much oh we want to find new chemical material binding to targets that are very challenging. And so that brings up a couple uh kind of tactical issues. Um one of them is that classically folks don't screen large numbers of protein targets. They're usually interested in finding chemical matter for something that's like really hard. Uh and and and they have maybe tried a bunch of other techniques and they haven't worked out. So okay, let's try a DEL screen because we don't have anything. Then they'll go off and make uh the protein that they're going to try to screen and they'll put a lot of work into it because it feels like kind of a lift to do a DEL screen. And so maybe they might spend two to six months growing big batches of the protein that they care about, doing a bunch of purifications. Maybe they're going to run some functional assays to convince themselves that oh, it's really got to be this good uh for us to go off and run this screen. Um and then when they run the screen, they're going to try to maximize their chances of getting pretty good chemical material. And so then the incentive drives into a place where we want we want a big DEL like we want a lot of diversity. And so if you go looking at uh folks who are offering CRO services or internal DEL groups a lot of times they'll push into these very large DELs uh and hopes and that and that's their motivation and and it makes a lot of sense. We just want to get tons and tons of you know active chemical material across large numbers of proteins. turns.zh: 但我想说的一件事是，呃，当 DELs 被发明时，呃，那绝对是在测序更昂贵的时代，做测序实验感觉像是一个大的后勤和财务波动。呃，然后当你当时构建技术，然后指向它所指向的问题时，非常像是哦，我们想要找到与非常具有挑战性的靶标结合的新化学材料。所以这带来了几个战术问题。呃，其中之一是，传统上人们不会筛选大量的蛋白质靶标。他们通常感兴趣的是为非常难的东西找到化学物质。呃，他们可能尝试了一堆其他技术，但没有成功。所以好吧，让我们尝试 DEL 筛选，因为我们什么都没有。然后他们会去制造他们要筛选的蛋白质，他们会投入大量工作，因为做 DEL 筛选感觉像是一种提升。所以也许他们可能会花两到六个月生长他们关心的大批量蛋白质，进行一堆纯化。也许他们会运行一些功能测定来说服自己，哦，它真的必须这么好，我们才能去运行这个筛选。呃，然后当他们运行筛选时，他们会试图最大化获得相当好的化学材料的机会。所以激励驱动到一个地方，我们想要一个大的 DEL，就像我们想要很多多样性。所以如果你去看提供 CRO 服务的人或内部 DEL 团队，很多时候他们会推动这些非常大的 DELs，呃，希望如此，这就是他们的动机，这很有道理。我们所做的非常非常不同的事情是，呃，你知道，我们筛选成吨成吨的蛋白质，我们不太受驱动于试图为某个可能对项目高度感兴趣的特定蛋白质靶标找到单个结合物。我们只是想获得成吨成吨的活性化学材料，跨越大量蛋白质。所以在那里我们可以很好地识别我们的 DELs 的行为，因为我们的每一个化学库都被筛选针对数百个靶标。所以你更好地表征化学库。

turns.en: We know very, very well, and so we start to encounter lots of these motifs that are quirks of the chemistry that we designed or maybe the manufacturing process. turns.en: So, when you're trying to drug something, I talked a little bit earlier about how you've got a protein of interest in your body and you're going to try to interact, you affect its behavior in some way. There are a couple different things that are currently on the market that people use. One thing that's common is antibodies, which are made by cells. They're large molecules. And by large, they're big enough that they have a really hard time getting inside cells. They also have a really hard time being in a pill. So if you have like an antibody treatment or one of these protein treatments like GLP-1 treatments, you're going to have to have kind of an injection. It can affect certain proteins that are easy for them to get to. But there's other ones inside the cell that drive a lot of disease that are quite challenging for those. It is kind of more appealing in a lot of ways to instead of have this big thing that's a protein to have a little tiny chemical. And tiny chemicals, small molecules here, are things that can be in pills. They can go inside your cells and affect behaviors. They do make up most of drugs. If you've got any pills in your house, they're almost certainly small molecules. And of the different machine learning drug discovery groups that are going after treatments in a general sense, we have made—we as in all of you, life scientists in the 21st century—have made pretty good progress on being able to predict and enable the behaviors of protein type drugs. So you've got a bunch of antibody companies like Isomorphic does this or like Chai or Nava. There's all these groups of very good, very smart people pushing on these particular problems, and I think part of that is because we understand or have enough data for protein behaviors that make it reasonably effective for these companies to do these designs. Our thesis is that those capabilities are really not here for small molecule approaches. And so that was one reason why we built this company: we felt that we could go after it in a meaningful way.
turns.zh: 所以，当你试图药物化某物时，我之前谈过你体内有一个感兴趣的蛋白质，你要尝试相互作用，以某种方式影响它的行为。目前市场上有几种不同的东西人们使用。常见的一种是抗体，由细胞制造。它们是大分子。所谓大，它们大到很难进入细胞内部。它们也很难做成药丸。所以如果你有抗体治疗或像 GLP-1 治疗这样的蛋白质治疗，你将不得不注射。它可以影响某些容易到达的蛋白质。但细胞内还有其他驱动许多疾病的蛋白质，对这些来说相当具有挑战性。在很多方面，与其用这个大东西——蛋白质，不如用一个小化学物质，这更有吸引力。小化学物质，这里的小分子，是可以放在药丸里的东西。它们可以进入你的细胞并影响行为。它们确实构成了大多数药物。如果你家里有任何药丸，它们几乎肯定是小分子。在那些一般性地追求治疗的不同的机器学习药物发现小组中，我们已经取得了——我们指的是你们所有人，21 世纪的生命科学家——在能够预测和实现蛋白质类型药物行为方面取得了相当好的进展。所以你有一堆抗体公司，比如 Isomorphic 做这个，或者像 Chai 或 Nava。有所有这些非常优秀、非常聪明的人在这些特定问题上推进，我认为部分原因是我们理解或有足够的数据来了解蛋白质行为，使得这些公司能够相当有效地进行这些设计。我们的论点是，这些能力对于小分子方法来说真的还不存在。所以这就是我们建立这家公司的原因之一：我们觉得我们可以以有意义的方式去追求它。

turns.en: So the path through the regulatory barriers for small molecules can be a little bit more fraught than those for antibodies. And so antibodies we know pretty well right now about how they behave in the body and what they are likely to cause problems and what they're not. And as a medicinal chemist, a person whose job it is to develop these molecules to get them from something that looks okay in a tube to something that you would feel confident enough to give to a human being. There are a lot of these pitfalls and they have to do a lot of work to avoid these pitfalls. turns.zh: 你可以拿，是的，你可以拿我们的二元标签，你可以自己做。所有的评估，一切，都在 Polaris 上，那是一个由 Recursion 运营的非营利组织。它在那里供任何人使用。请使用它，我们故意发布它，希望社区能好好利用它。

turns.en: Do you think though the structure of this data set was fundamentally limited in a way that maybe without some external augmentation, you're not going to be able to do any better than what people have pretty much already done.

Because if we all have models that really understand truly understand like the physics of the interactions between the amino acids of the small molecules, then it doesn't really matter what the distribution of the small molecule training set would look like if they're really good at this, you know, and I think when we see when we see structural model predictions and folks say, "Oh, well, you know, I've got this time split on the PDB, for example, and you know, you know, our model's never seen these molecules or this protein before, and then hopefully we can, you know, kind of use this understanding to make reasonable folds." Like that's very much in the spirit of being able to make the predictions on this stuff cuz no one has seen these especially our internal molecules like no one's seen those before.
turns.zh: 我认为如果你有真正完美的结构理解，或者非常好的结构模型，那么你应该能在这上面做得不错，对吧？因为如果我们都有模型真正理解小分子氨基酸之间相互作用的物理，那么如果它们真的很擅长这个，小分子训练集的分布是什么样就不重要了。我认为当我们看到结构模型预测时，人们说，哦，好吧，你知道，我在 PDB 上有一个时间分割，例如，你知道，我们的模型从未见过这些分子或这个蛋白质，然后希望我们能利用这种理解来做出合理的折叠。这非常符合能够对这些东西做出预测的精神，因为没有人见过这些，尤其是我们的内部小分子，没有人见过那些。

turns.en: Can you tell us about that, and some of the learnings there, and especially how you evaluated that model and all the care you put into it?
turns.zh: 你能给我们讲讲那个吗？还有其中的一些经验教训，特别是你如何评估那个模型，以及你投入的所有心血？

turns.en: Hermes is a model that is the original brainchild of a data scientist at Le named Mike Kleiner, Max Kleinesser, and also Sean Francis Line, and Andrew Bleven, of course, is the CTO there. The thinking originally was that we had a bunch of data and we were thinking about how to split it and different training regimes, so we wanted to come up with a model that was really, really dead simple so that we could do lots of potential experimental iterations. Its purpose wasn't to be a state-of-the-art model; it was like, we want to try stuff fast. So we built Hermes, and then the basic architecture of Hermes is two different embeddings. One of them is an evolutionary scale modeling, ESM, embedding—that's a protein embedding that comes from a group that was at Meta and then went off to start their own company, and then they got picked up by Chan Zuckerberg more recently.
turns.zh: Hermes 是一个模型，最初是由 Le 的一位数据科学家 Mike Kleiner、Max Kleinesser，还有 Sean Francis Line 构思的，当然 Andrew Bleven 是那里的 CTO。最初的想法是，我们有一堆数据，我们在考虑如何划分数据以及不同的训练方案，所以我们想出一个非常非常简单的模型，这样我们可以进行大量潜在的实验迭代。它的目的不是成为最先进的模型，而是像，我们想快速尝试东西。所以我们构建了 Hermes，然后 Hermes 的基本架构是两个不同的嵌入。一个是进化尺度建模，ESM 嵌入——那是一种蛋白质嵌入，来自一个曾在 Meta 的团队，然后他们离开去创办了自己的公司，最近被 Chan Zuckerberg 收购了。

turns.en: We had Alex Reeves on the podcast, so we can throw back to that episode if you want to hear more—go back a few years. Yeah, thank you, Alex, if you're listening.
turns.zh: 我们播客请过 Alex Reeves，所以如果你想了解更多，可以回顾那一期——回到几年前。是的，谢谢你，Alex，如果你在听的话。

turns.en: So we did that for the protein side. And then we had a different embedding called Kvera, which is basically like an X token predictor chemistry kind of thing on the other side.
turns.zh: 所以我们在蛋白质方面用了那个。然后我们有一个不同的嵌入叫 Kvera，基本上就像是一个 X 令牌预测器化学之类的东西在另一边。

turns.en: Something which predicts SMILES or—
turns.zh: 预测 SMILES 的东西还是——

turns.en: That's right. Yeah. Just predicts SMILES tokens. And so that's it. These very, very two simple embeddings, and then we just put them together with cross attention, and that was it. And then we used it to predict a binary label.
turns.zh: 没错。是的。就是预测 SMILES 令牌。就这样。这两个非常非常简单的嵌入，然后我们用交叉注意力把它们放在一起，就这样。然后我们用它来预测一个二元标签。

turns.en: Simplest possible thing.
turns.zh: 最简单的东西。

turns.en: It's incredibly simple. Very, very small, and then we trained some data on it.
turns.zh: 它非常简单。非常非常小，然后我们在上面训练了一些数据。

turns.en: Actually, you know, not the simplest. You could have done an MLP after those, right, instead of cross attention. So why attention?
turns.zh: 其实，你知道，不是最简单的。你可以在那些之后做一个 MLP，对吧，而不是交叉注意力。那为什么用注意力？

turns.en: The thinking with the attention was had to do with some other experiences that we'd had with graph convolutional-like graph models for protein structure. And one thing that we noticed is if you've got these sorts of graphs and there's a couple models that do this at other work that we had done, we had scrambled the positional coordinates of those and performance for some of those models more or less stayed the same. And that made us think that attention was super critical. And so we ended up just making sure that the model was at least—at least what we hoped is that it would be looking at the different parts of the proteins to small molecule structures that could be useful here.
turns.zh: 注意力的思考与我们之前在蛋白质结构的图卷积类图模型上的一些其他经验有关。我们注意到的一件事是，如果你有这类图，并且在我们做过的其他工作中，有几个模型这样做，我们打乱了那些的位置坐标，而其中一些模型的性能或多或少保持不变。这让我们认为注意力非常关键。所以我们最终只是确保模型至少——至少我们希望的是，它会查看蛋白质的不同部分到小分子结构，这可能在这里有用。

turns.en: So this is, I think, oftentimes known as the Picasso problem in image generation, where, let's say, CNNs, for example, were famous for a while where you could scramble just the features of a picture—like Picasso, like flip the nose around or just rotate the eyes or something—and the CNN would still depict, oh, this is a Picasso, because it just picked up on individual local features rather than some sort of global structure. And this has been a problem in small molecule drug discovery for a while, where oftentimes it picks up on local motifs and then it doesn't have any global understanding of the topology. So especially for something like DELs, where you have this combinatorial structure of individual building blocks, you could imagine the model learning each building block independently and then essentially just decomposing into the sum of three building blocks or something. I mean, it's a simple concept.
turns.zh: 所以这就是我认为在图像生成中经常被称为毕加索问题的情况，比如说，CNN 曾经出名一段时间，你可以打乱图片的特征——像毕加索那样，比如把鼻子翻转过来或者旋转眼睛之类的——而 CNN 仍然会描述，哦，这是毕加索，因为它只是捕捉到了个别的局部特征，而不是某种全局结构。这在小分子药物发现中已经是一个问题一段时间了，它经常捕捉到局部基序，然后对拓扑结构没有任何全局理解。所以特别是对于像 DEL 这样的东西，你有单个构建块的组合结构，你可以想象模型独立学习每个构建块，然后基本上只是分解为三个构建块的总和之类的。我的意思是，这是一个简单的概念。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. So cross attention in some sense forces certain molecules to interact with certain residues in a protein.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。所以交叉注意力在某种意义上是强制某些分子与蛋白质中的某些残基相互作用。

turns.en: Yep. Or at least maybe not forces but provides the offer. Think about it. It's an inductive bias.
turns.zh: 是的。或者至少可能不是强制，而是提供机会。想想看。这是一种归纳偏置。

turns.en: Yeah. Kind of what you're getting at is, you know, we were thinking about how to evaluate this, and so we had done some of the similar tricks that we did over with the Kaggle competition, where we had training sets and data that we generated internally, and then we'd looked at chemical libraries that were further away. But then also we wanted to think about splits to kind of probe Hermes' behavior. And so because DELs have this combinatorial approach, you can do the same thing where you might share certain building blocks. And so we do that, and of course performance is better, which we suspect is due to memorization. But the other thing is you can imagine that there are building blocks that are very similar to one another, that if you're just trying to split on the identity of those, then you might have things that are close enough that memorization or some other cheat mode might convert predictive power. And so we came up with a scheme where we then did basically clustering of these different building blocks. We had building block clusters on similarity. And that way we would just avoid entire clusters from being overlap between test and train. And so when you do that, then you know the performance does drop.
turns.zh: 是的。你大概想说的是，你知道，我们在考虑如何评估这个，所以我们做了一些类似的技巧，就像我们在 Kaggle 竞赛中做的那样，我们有内部生成的训练集和数据，然后我们查看了更远的化学库。但然后我们还想考虑划分来探测 Hermes 的行为。因为 DEL 有这种组合方法，你可以做同样的事情，你可能会共享某些构建块。所以我们这样做，当然性能更好，我们怀疑这是由于记忆。但另一件事是，你可以想象有些构建块彼此非常相似，如果你只是试图根据它们的身份来划分，那么你可能会得到足够接近的东西，记忆或其他作弊模式可能会转换预测能力。所以我们想出了一个方案，然后我们基本上对这些不同的构建块进行聚类。我们有基于相似性的构建块聚类。这样我们就可以避免整个聚类在测试和训练之间重叠。所以当你这样做时，你知道性能确实会下降。

turns.en: So one thing that you might be alluding to is we have—you know, we use lots of reasonable baselines here that we're really worried about. And so for almost everything that we do, we'll use like XGBoost, right? You should use something like that just to see how it's going.
turns.zh: 所以你可能会提到的一件事是，我们有——你知道，我们在这里使用了很多合理的基线，我们真的很担心。所以对于我们做的几乎所有事情，我们都会使用像 XGBoost，对吧？你应该使用类似的东西来看看进展如何。

turns.en: Right. Yeah. Every—yeah. The classic young machine learner practitioner, they spend six months optimizing their favorite model and then someone walks by and does like XGBoost, random forest, and they're like, "Oh yeah, that just beat like six months of work." Oh yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。是的。每个——是的。经典的年轻机器学习实践者，他们花六个月优化他们最喜欢的模型，然后有人走过，做了像 XGBoost、随机森林，他们就像，“哦是的，那刚刚打败了六个月的工作。”哦是的。是的。

turns.en: Yeah. And so we did these different split regimes to try to evaluate how well things would do relative to like actually boost performance.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们做了这些不同的划分方案，试图评估事情相对于实际提升性能会做得如何。

turns.en: And so one thing that was really, really gratifying to see is that you see XGBoost drop steadily as you get further and further away with these building block cluster approaches. It's like if you share two building blocks, it's a certain level. If you only share one, it gets worse. If you share one, you know, only none, it's worse. And if you do building block, it's even worse than that. And then we compared that to the Hermes performance, which was pretty steady across all these different regimes.
turns.zh: 所以一件非常非常令人欣慰的事情是，你看到 XGBoost 随着你通过这些构建块聚类方法越来越远而稳步下降。就像如果你共享两个构建块，它处于某个水平。如果你只共享一个，它会变差。如果你共享一个，你知道，只有没有，它更差。如果你做构建块，它比那更差。然后我们将其与 Hermes 的性能进行比较，后者在所有这些不同的方案中相当稳定。

turns.en: I see.
turns.zh: 我明白了。

turns.en: Yeah. So it made us think like, oh yeah, you know, you've really got to get pretty far out of distribution for XGBoost to really tank. And that's something that we haven't—you know, we haven't—it's in a couple plots and some work that we published. We haven't yelled about it too much.
turns.zh: 是的。所以这让我们觉得，哦是的，你知道，你真的必须相当远离分布才能让 XGBoost 真正崩溃。这是我们没有——你知道，我们没有——它在几个图表和我们发表的一些工作中。我们没有过多地大声宣扬。

turns.en: Wait, do I—I thought—don't you have a blog post like XGBoost is all you do? That's why we did that.
turns.zh: 等等，我——我以为——你不是有一篇博客文章叫 XGBoost 就是你所做的一切吗？这就是为什么我们这样做。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Running those splits is something that we've put a lot of thought into, trying to figure out, okay, how do you stop your models from really memorizing and remembering things? This might be a good time for a little bit of a detour, but referencing another one of your blog posts which I found absolutely hilarious from my own personal experience. I have seen machine learning models fail, like pick up on so many weird detractors, and your blog post about molecule ownership or authorship was a really fun story.
turns.zh: 运行那些拆分是我们花了很多心思去思考的事情，试图弄清楚，好吧，你怎么阻止你的模型真正记住和记住东西？这可能是一个很好的时机来稍微绕个弯，但引用你另一篇博客文章，我从自己的个人经历中发现它绝对搞笑。我见过机器学习模型失败，比如捕捉到许多奇怪的干扰因素，而你关于分子所有权或作者身份的博客文章是一个非常有趣的故事。

turns.en: The Clever Hans post. Yeah. So many years ago, my co-founder Andrew Blevens and I were at Recursion looking at a small molecule on a screen, and then a medicinal chemist walked by us. This guy named Mike Karesi. And Mike was like, "Hey, looks like a Steuart Triber molecule." And then we were like, "Oh no, you can tell just by walking by like who made this? That's horrifying." And then that haunted Andrew in particular for like many years. Like it was like six or seven years. And we joked, you know, I don't know, every couple of months we're out for beers like man we really should figure out like how bad this problem is.
turns.zh: 《聪明汉斯》那篇。是的。很多年前，我和我的联合创始人安德鲁·布莱文斯在 Recursion 公司，看着屏幕上的一个小分子，然后一位药物化学家从我们身边走过。这家伙叫迈克·卡雷西。迈克说：“嘿，看起来像斯图尔特·特里伯的分子。”然后我们就像，“哦不，你只要走过就能看出这是谁做的？太可怕了。”然后这件事尤其困扰了安德鲁很多年。大概有六七年。我们开玩笑，你知道，每隔几个月我们出去喝酒时就会说，天哪，我们真的应该弄清楚这个问题有多严重。

turns.en: Why is that a problem?
turns.zh: 为什么那是个问题？

turns.en: Okay so it's a problem where it's very easy to imagine you're going to try to train models to understand chemistry. So you're going to get the data from lots of groups because it's very tempting to get data from lots of groups. And if the models can identify the chemist by looking at the molecule alone, then maybe the models can infer chemist intent, which means maybe they don't learn anything at all. And so,
turns.zh: 好吧，问题在于很容易想象你会尝试训练模型来理解化学。所以你会从很多小组获取数据，因为从很多小组获取数据非常诱人。如果模型仅通过观察分子就能识别化学家，那么也许模型可以推断化学家的意图，这意味着也许它们根本学不到任何东西。所以，

turns.en: well, they did learn something.
turns.zh: 嗯，它们确实学到了一些东西。

turns.en: They learn something. Yeah. Yeah. They don't learn physics, right? They're not learning the thing you're trying to get them to learn. And so we were really afraid of this.
turns.zh: 它们学到了一些东西。是的。是的。它们没有学到物理，对吧？它们没有学到你试图让它们学的东西。所以我们真的很害怕这个。

turns.en: They learned that certain chemists are better than other woods.
turns.zh: 它们学到了某些化学家比其他化学家更好。

turns.en: Yeah. We learned all kinds of stuff, but maybe to set this up for the audience. So we went out and we published this over Christmas. You can look it up. We have a leaderboard. We have a goofy online game you can play. But we downloaded all chemicals from all chemists at Kemble, which is the biggest repository of these things and their activities. Every chemist who published more than I think it was 30 papers and 600 molecules. So you get all molecules and all the stuff. It's 1,815 chemists and then we train a classifier to predict a chemist from looking at the molecule alone and we got a top five accuracy of 60%. It's a very very easy problem.
turns.zh: 是的。我们学到了各种各样的东西，但也许为观众设定一下。所以我们出去，我们在圣诞节期间发表了这篇。你可以查一下。我们有一个排行榜。我们有一个愚蠢的在线游戏你可以玩。但我们从 Kemble 下载了所有化学家的所有化学品，这是这些东西及其活性的最大存储库。每个发表超过我认为是 30 篇论文和 600 个分子的化学家。所以你得到所有分子和所有东西。有 1,815 位化学家，然后我们训练了一个分类器，仅通过观察分子来预测化学家，我们得到了 60% 的前五准确率。这是一个非常非常容易的问题。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah. It's super easy for the models to do. Where they get confused is where you have two chemists who were on the same publications and were at the same institution. And so we think it's very likely is that there is a distinctive chemical signature style that individuals have when they make molecules. And then when those individuals have students or trainees, then they adopt some fraction of that, you know, and so that was that seemed pretty pretty clear to us. And so that was horrifying enough on its own. And this is a data set that many many academic projects many PhDs have trained on, tried to predict on, find patterns and this is really like a major data set for the field.
turns.zh: 是的。模型做起来超级容易。它们困惑的地方是当你有两位化学家在同一篇出版物上并且在同一机构。所以我们认为很可能的是，个人在制造分子时有一种独特的化学签名风格。然后当这些人有学生或实习生时，他们会采用其中的一部分，你知道，所以这对我们来说似乎非常清楚。所以这本身就足够可怕了。这是一个许多学术项目、许多博士训练过、试图预测、寻找模式的数据集，这真的是该领域的一个主要数据集。

turns.en: Yeah. Like if you are not generating your own data, you're using this. And then if you are generating your own data, then you are probably victim to this because your organization probably has multiple chemists who have their own distinctive chemical styles and that they are using their styles to go after different types of projects.
turns.zh: 是的。就像如果你不生成自己的数据，你就在使用这个。然后如果你在生成自己的数据，那么你可能也是这个的受害者，因为你的组织可能有多个化学家，他们有自己的独特化学风格，并且他们使用自己的风格去追求不同类型的项目。

turns.en: But the key here I think is that those chemists also tend to solve similar problems. Like I might have a career here and I have a style but I also am working on a class of problems, right? And so your style is also, you're learning the style instead of the problem. You're learning the style, you're learning the sociology of the problem. And the other thing that you're learning is that when you're a chemist at these organizations, you know, ordering a molecule to be manufactured and tested is kind of a pain, right? So what will happen is you will make many many choices of things you will not pursue, and you do not write those down. Oh yeah, it would be dumb to do that. And it's like, yeah, that's their motivation. Like our team couldn't just make it. Like they could say like, we could do this, but then they would cost too much. Or the lab team will say, the chemistry team will say, "No, we can't make it now." Or, you know, like we don't have the building blocks on
turns.zh: 但这里的关键我认为是那些化学家也倾向于解决类似的问题。就像我可能在这里有一个职业生涯，我有一种风格，但我也在从事一类问题，对吧？所以你的风格也是，你在学习风格而不是问题。你在学习风格，你在学习问题的社会学。你学到的另一件事是，当你在这些组织做化学家时，你知道，订购一个分子来制造和测试有点痛苦，对吧？所以会发生的是你会做出许多许多你不会追求的选择，而你不会写下那些。哦是的，那样做很愚蠢。就像，是的，那是他们的动机。就像我们的团队就是做不到。他们可以说，我们可以做这个，但那样成本太高。或者实验室团队会说，化学团队会说：“不，我们现在做不了。”或者，你知道，就像我们没有构建块在

turns.zh: 所以某些失败模式，比如任何容易组装的东西也容易拆解，对 ADMET 性质不利。你能扩展的空间有限，因为你已经用掉了一些组合构建模块，等等。总之，这在长期超出库的泛化方面有什么限制？

turns.en: I think a lot of it is going to be somewhat dependent on building block availability and one's willingness to go into custom synthesis. So, especially for the fine-grained mapping stuff, being able to say, move a nitrogen all the way around the ring at all of those positions, is something that's very, very desirable, but it's also something that's pretty unlikely that you're going to get commercially for all sorts of building blocks you're currently generating. So is that going to be a failing mode? For sure. Yes. Yes, I would love to be able to get more of those and beef up our custom synthesis. That's something that we're looking at. But right now, trying to get those is challenging.
turns.zh: 我觉得很大程度上取决于构建模块的可获得性，以及是否愿意做定制合成。所以，尤其是对于精细映射这类工作，能够说把氮原子沿着环在所有那些位置上都移动一遍，是非常非常理想的，但对你目前生成的各种构建模块来说，商业上不太可能都拿到。所以这会成为失败模式吗？当然会。是的。是的，我很希望能拿到更多这类东西，加强我们的定制合成。这是我们正在考虑的事。但现在，想拿到这些很有挑战性。

turns.en: One critique that Claude might be thinking about, in terms of molecules easy to put together and disassemble: for many years, the most common way to attach building blocks between DEL chemistries is amide bonds or peptide bonds. And so those are quite digestible in the body. But in the past few years — really the past four-ish years — there has been a really nice fluorescence of chemistries that are friendly to DNA, that don't destroy it during the attachment process, because that's very important, that will give you carbon-carbon bonds, carbon-nitrogen bonds, these kinds of things. So it's actually pretty good for workaday simple chemistry. Yeah. So I'm actually not too worried about that part. I'm more worried about building block diversity than the sources for that.
turns.zh: Claude 可能会想到的一个批评，关于分子容易组装也容易拆解：很多年来，在 DEL 化学之间连接构建模块最常见的方式是酰胺键或肽键。这些在体内相当容易被消化。但在过去几年——其实是过去四年左右——出现了一波非常好的对 DNA 友好的化学方法，在连接过程中不会破坏 DNA，因为这一点非常重要，它们能给你碳碳键、碳氮键这类东西。所以对于日常的简单化学来说其实相当不错。对，所以我其实不太担心这部分。我更担心的是构建模块的多样性，而不是它的来源。

turns.en: What about ADMET properties in general? You've been focusing very much on binding.
turns.zh: 那总体上的 ADMET 性质呢？你一直非常专注于结合。

turns.en: We have. Yeah. So for projects that we've done, trying to look at reasonable ADMET and PKPD properties — for what it's worth, we've gone directly from chemical library hits to good PKPD in a mouse in six months with a very small number of medchem cycles. So at least the chemical matter that we currently have, or at least those few series that we did that for, turned out pretty good in our hands. I guess we will continue to see how that modeling looks, and also of course we want to do more of these ADMET target models and then think about how to incorporate other types of more emergent models along with our designs.
turns.zh: 是的。对。就我们做过的项目而言，试着去看合理的 ADMET 和 PKPD 性质——值得一提的是，我们直接从化合物库命中物做到了小鼠体内良好的 PKPD，只用了六个月，而且药物化学循环次数非常少。所以至少我们目前手上的化学物质，或者至少我们做过的那几个系列，在我们手里结果相当不错。我想我们会继续看这种建模效果如何，当然我们也想做更多这类 ADMET 靶点模型，然后思考如何把其他更新兴的模型类型和我们的设计结合起来。

turns.en: Was that speed driven by your ability to create custom local combinatorial libraries, or what allowed you to get there in six months?
turns.zh: 这种速度是由你们创建定制本地组合库的能力驱动的，还是别的什么让你们能在六个月内做到？

turns.en: So when we designed those chemical libraries at the beginning, we very much optimized that space for drug-likeness, and so we think that's part of it — that was a really good starting point. When we do our chemical library designs, we have this kind of like Thompson sampling-level approach where we come up with an optimization function. You say, okay, well, I want the libraries to have these properties. And so some of those properties are going to be, I want to bind these things, I want to avoid these things. And then some of these properties are going to be — oh, there's other ADMET model approaches that you can use to make predictions about how your chemical matter might turn out. And so you put that as part of the optimization function. And then what you do is you say, okay, of all the chemicals that I could make given my geometry, I don't want to make that many. I want to make a smaller number. And so you basically set up and generate a bunch of synthetic libraries and then you score them on this optimization function. And so we did that with this library, and the starting material looked pretty good. So I'm sure that we'll continue to do that.
turns.zh: 我们在最开始设计那些化合物库时，非常针对类药性优化了那个空间，所以我们认为这是部分原因——那是一个非常好的起点。当我们做化合物库设计时，我们有这种类似 Thompson 采样层面的方法，先提出一个优化函数。你说，好，我希望这些库具有这些性质。其中一些性质会是：我想结合这些东西，我想避免这些东西。然后另一些性质会是——哦，还有别的 ADMET 模型方法可以用来预测你的化学物质可能会怎样。于是你把它作为优化函数的一部分。然后你要做的是：好，在给定我的几何结构下我能造出的所有化合物里，我不想造那么多，我想造更少的数量。所以你基本上就是设置并生成一堆合成库，然后用这个优化函数给它们打分。我们对这个库就是这么做的，起始物看起来相当不错。所以我相信我们会继续这么做。

turns.en: Along those same lines, has anything that you've done made it to — so it made it to animals and —
turns.zh: 顺着这个思路，你们做的任何东西有没有推进到——就是推进到动物，然后——

turns.en: So PKPD in a mouse is that. Yeah.
turns.zh: 小鼠体内的 PKPD 就是那个。对。

turns.en: So what that means is, can you dose the mouse with the thing and then see how it gets into the mouse's body and tissues?
turns.zh: 所以那意味着，你能给小鼠用药，然后看它如何进入小鼠的身体和组织？

turns.en: Yeah. So PKPD is pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, meaning how does the body move the drug through the body.
turns.zh: 对。PKPD 就是药代动力学、药效动力学，意思是身体如何让药物在体内移动。

turns.en: Yep. And then are there biomarkers of the drug's intended activity? And so what that means here is this is a drug, this is a compound we're working on for inflammation.
turns.zh: 对。然后有没有药物预期活性的生物标志物？所以这里的意思是，这是一种药物，这是我们正在研究的一个用于炎症的化合物。

turns.en: And so we were following up cytokine levels in mouse blood, and they did what we wanted them to do and expected them to do based on the targets of the drug.
turns.zh: 于是我们追踪了小鼠血液中的细胞因子水平，它们确实按照我们基于药物靶点的预期发挥了作用。

turns.en: So, Sean likes to ask when money. I want to ask when people—
turns.zh: 所以，Sean 喜欢问什么时候能赚钱。我想问的是，什么时候人们——

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, for those we talked to, we have a couple of these things that we're talking to folks about partnering up to spin up new entities to go chase them down.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，对于那些我们谈过的人，我们有几个这样的项目，正在和一些人讨论合作，成立新的实体去推进它们。

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: And so, yeah, and of course, like all these things take some time. You've got to do these traditional things forward—once you declare what's called a development candidate, then you've got to do a bunch of other work about manufacturing and additional safety work before you can get into people. So all these things take a little longer.
turns.zh: 所以，是的，当然，所有这些事情都需要一些时间。你得推进这些传统流程——一旦你宣布了所谓的开发候选药物，你还得做一堆关于生产制造和额外安全性方面的工作，才能进入人体试验。所以这些事情都需要更长一点的时间。

turns.en: Yeah. And so you're going to spin out the idea is to spin out a—so people maybe even internal, they will say like, I really want to take this thing to market or try to get it, like take it to the next step.
turns.zh: 是的。所以你们打算拆分出去，想法是拆分出一个——所以也许甚至内部的人会说，我真的很想把这个东西推向市场，或者试着把它推进到下一步。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, I mean, one way that we kind of think about it is, you know, we built this really great engine for data generation and model training, and now as we've talked about, these reinforcement learning reasoning approaches. And in most other domains, when you build an engine to go do that stuff, to go help on those problems, the subset that you're generating along the way is not itself intrinsically valuable. No one wants to sell reasoning traces about political theory,
turns.zh: 是的。是的，我的意思是，我们思考这件事的一种方式是，你知道，我们打造了这个非常出色的引擎，用于数据生成和模型训练，现在正如我们讨论过的，还有这些强化学习推理方法。在大多数其他领域，当你构建一个引擎去做这些事情、去帮助解决这些问题时，你在这个过程中生成的子集本身并不具有内在价值。没有人想卖关于政治理论的推理轨迹，

turns.en: but like there are going to be little bits of gold that we have generated as a consequence of doing all the screening
turns.zh: 但就像我们在做所有这些筛选的过程中，会生成一些小小的金子，

turns.en: because you're actually reasoning about not only that this model is good—or sorry, this molecule is good—but that this here is why that's good. Here is why that's good, and here is chemical material that is proprietary to us that has, you know, activities that are in protein target classes that others might find hard to drug, right? And so you've got starting material for—you know, right now we have starting material that looks pretty selective to us for, I think, like 700 targets. Like it's an enormous number. You don't want to chase all those down, but you know, as opportunities, they are all opportunities with different levels of economic value capture and desirability. And so you think, all right, well, we got all this stuff. Like, let's see what we can get out. Let's see what we can get out of it. Discovery is like a small percentage of the total cost of developing a drug, and you can argue that, well—
turns.zh: 因为你实际上不仅在推理这个模型很好——抱歉，这个分子很好——而且在推理这里为什么它好。这里是为什么它好，而这里是对我们专有的化学材料，它在我们认为别人可能难以成药的蛋白质靶点类别中具有活性，对吧？所以你有了起始材料——你知道，现在我们有的起始材料，在我看来对大约 700 个靶点都相当有选择性。这是个巨大的数字。你不想把它们全部推进，但你知道，作为机会，它们都是具有不同程度经济价值捕获和可取性的机会。所以你想，好吧，我们有了所有这些材料。让我们看看能从中得到什么。让我们看看能从中得到什么。药物发现只占开发药物总成本的一小部分，你可以争辩说，好吧——

turns.en: you have a lot—any given discovery is cheap maybe, but because of the failures you have a lot of them. So but even then, you know—
turns.zh: 你有很多——任何一次发现也许很便宜，但由于失败，你有很多次发现。所以但即便如此，你知道——

turns.en: to get one drug, one drug, like all the steps of a single drug candidate
turns.zh: 要得到一款药，一款药，就像单个候选药物的所有步骤

turns.en: yeah
turns.zh: 是的

turns.en: that is successful is maybe, you know, on the low side 200 million, on the high side a billion, um, depending on who you have to test on and lots of other factors. But and then you know the discovery is a couple million. So so are you tackling the right problem here?
turns.zh: 一个成功的候选药物，你知道，低的话大概 2 亿美元，高的话 10 亿美元，嗯，取决于你要在谁身上测试以及很多其他因素。但然后你知道，发现阶段只是几百万美元。所以，你在这里解决的是正确的问题吗？

turns.en: Um, and so I think there are a number of early discovery problems that are worth that much, you know, like reasonable amounts. And so what does that mean? There's a bunch of targets right now with like really good genetic evidence that are very challenging to drug with small molecules.
turns.zh: 嗯，所以我认为有一些早期发现的问题值那么多钱，你知道，合理的金额。那这意味着什么呢？现在有一堆靶点，有非常好的遗传学证据，但用小分子非常难以成药。

turns.en: Um, you know, a pretty straightforward example is, uh, for a lot of these, um, uh, kind of cytokine inflammatory indications, folks are using antibodies to drug them and going after a small molecule therapeutic that you could take as a pill instead of an infusion, one that doesn't require, uh, like cold chain, you know, transport, uh, to get to different patient populations. Like having those things is enormously desirable,
turns.zh: 嗯，你知道，一个很直接的例子是，呃，对于很多这些，嗯，呃，细胞因子炎症适应症，人们用抗体来治疗，而去追求一种小分子疗法，你可以作为药片服用，而不是输液，一种不需要，呃，像冷链，你知道，运输，呃，就能到达不同患者群体的疗法。拥有这些东西是非常可取的，

turns.en: meaning you have to have refrigerated trucks,
turns.zh: 意味着你得有冷藏卡车，

turns.en: right? Yeah. Like and like if you want to get these—if you want to get these antibody-based drugs to some of these folks, like this is like a very hard problem.
turns.zh: 对吧？是的。就像如果你想把这些——如果你想把这些基于抗体的药物送到其中一些人手中，这就像一个非常困难的问题。

turns.en: Yeah. And very expensive
turns.zh: 是的。而且非常昂贵

turns.en: and very expensive. And so and so folks are like really quite excited about, can you find a small molecule therapeutic that does the same thing, uh, that antibody against these—
turns.zh: 而且非常昂贵。所以所以人们真的非常兴奋，你能不能找到一种小分子疗法，做同样的事情，呃，那种针对这些的抗体——

turns.en: so there's some antibody, it's—it works.
turns.zh: 所以有一些抗体，它——它有效。

turns.en: Yep. And so we know it works.
turns.zh: 是的。所以我们知道它有效。

turns.en: and and so you're like, well, why can't we just go after the same target with a small molecule?
turns.zh: 然后然后你就想，好吧，为什么我们不能用一个小分子去针对同一个靶点呢？

turns.en: And it turns out that those proteins are very hard to drug for a variety of reasons, but we like to think that, you know, the technology that we're developing can get good material. And so we do in fact have selective material for a lot of these cytokines. And so that's one example of something that's like a very desirable target where, of course, like there's going to be much more, uh, capital requirements to like get it across the line to actually get it to market, but the interest is sufficiently high enough.
turns.zh: 事实证明，由于各种原因，这些蛋白质非常难以成药，但我们倾向于认为，你知道，我们正在开发的技术可以得到好的材料。所以我们确实对很多这些细胞因子有选择性材料。所以这是一个例子，一个非常可取的靶点，当然，要把它推进到真正上市，会有更多的，呃，资本需求，但兴趣足够高。

turns.en: So you're going to ruin the antibody market basically. I mean, if like if you can, like then it's good for some stuff, like it's great for some stuff, and like there's a lot of energy being thrown, you know, at those groups because we're good at protein folding, right? And so like they're making a lot of progress.
turns.zh: 所以基本上你们要毁掉抗体市场了。我的意思是，如果你能的话，那么它对某些东西是好的，对某些东西是很好的，而且你知道，有很多精力被投入到那些团队，因为我们擅长蛋白质折叠，对吧？所以他们正在取得很多进展。

turns.en: And maybe more broadly, I would say is like going after the right problem. It is a little bit of a lamppost problem, where the things where we can make enough scalable measurements in the life sciences are these early problems. We can't really run a million mice experiments, right? Like we can't run many millions of phase one trials. And so we're going to get better at that stuff. We're going to start to like go up these different layers of biological abstraction with like better data and better reasoning and physics models. But like right now, like the technologies that we have to really make the number of measurements that we need are going to be like these early approaches, I think.
turns.zh: 也许更广泛地说，我会说，要解决正确的问题。这有点像一个路灯问题，在生命科学中，我们能做足够多可扩展测量的地方是这些早期问题。我们没法真的做一百万次小鼠实验，对吧？就像我们没法做几百万次一期临床试验。所以我们会在这方面变得更好。我们会开始用更好的数据、更好的推理和物理模型，去攀登这些不同的生物抽象层次。但就像现在，我们真正需要做足够多测量的技术，我认为会是这些早期方法。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah. And I would argue also that you can, if you have an oracle, some AI oracle that says, oh, this, like all the ADMET properties will be good, and this generalizes to exactly this population. So you have this oracle filter, then all of your failures in clinical trials go away.
turns.zh: 是的。我还会争辩说，如果你有一个预言机，某个 AI 预言机说，哦，这个，所有 ADMET 属性都会很好，而且这正好泛化到这个人群。所以你有这个预言机过滤器，那么你在临床试验中的所有失败都会消失。

turns.en: Yeah, you can imagine a world where you can come up with an—or you have some new target that you know, some new evidence that covers, uh, and then the Oracle could give you small molecule material instantly that you would feel comfortable running straight to like a mouse study.
turns.zh: 是的，你可以想象一个世界，你可以提出一个——或者你有一些新靶点，你知道，一些新证据覆盖了，呃，然后预言机可以立即给你小分子材料，你会觉得可以直接拿去跑小鼠研究。

turns.en: Right. Right. Right. So, but so that requires training on data from mouse studies, clinical trials, whatever.
turns.zh: 对。对。对。所以，但那需要在来自小鼠研究、临床试验等的数据上训练。

turns.en: I mean, maybe, I mean, I could say definitely like ADMET properties if you're confident in the target and you need to make sure that it's not hitting all these other off targets.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，也许，我的意思是，我可以肯定地说，如果你对靶点有信心，ADMET 属性，你需要确保它不会命中所有其他这些脱靶靶点。

ts.sec: The Koseri Paradox of ML in Drug Discovery

turns.en: All right. Well, we're on everyone's favorite pet question. My favorite pet question is what I call the Koseri paradox of machine learning and discovery.
turns.zh: 好，我们现在来聊大家最喜欢的那个老生常谈的问题。我最喜欢的老生常谈，就是我称之为机器学习与发现中的“科塞里悖论”。

turns.en: Yes. Yes.
turns.zh: 对。对。

turns.en: Okay. So, Shri Kosari, great tweet. I love this tweet. He was on with us a few weeks ago. We hopefully will release his episode in the next few weeks.
turns.zh: 好。那么，Shri Kosari，那条推文很棒。我很喜欢那条推文。他几周前上过我们的节目。希望我们能在接下来几周内发布他那期。

turns.en: Sadly, I actually didn't even bring this up on the episode. I'm so disappointed.
turns.zh: 可惜的是，我在那期节目里居然都没提到这个。我太失望了。

turns.en: Anyway, but yeah, the tweet is basically: what is the business model in machine learning for drug discovery? Because in order to build a good machine learning model, you need lots of data and good high quality data at scale. You clearly have that. But then if you need that to train the model, like what do you need the model for? Because you just go collect the stuff and you clearly can collect this stuff quite well. So yeah, we talked a lot about data collection. We talked a lot about machine learning. And I'm actually kind of curious in some ways: like where does the actual machine learning—is it necessary for your business model?
turns.zh: 总之，那条推文大致是说：机器学习做药物发现的商业模式到底是什么？因为要构建一个好的机器学习模型，你需要大量数据，需要规模化、高质量的数据。你显然有这些数据。但如果你需要这些数据来训练模型，那你还要模型干什么？因为你直接去收集就行了，而你显然能把这些东西收集得相当好。所以，我们聊了很多数据收集，也聊了很多机器学习。我其实有点好奇：实际的机器学习——它对你们的商业模式是必需的吗？

turns.en: So I mean of course it would depend on the business model. I think if your only rationale is to go off and get good chemical material for a particular target, then of course Shri is right, right? You could get started if you had enough chemical material broadly cast across all these other targets in a way that can drive a deeper machine understanding of the chemical behaviors than the way by which you optimize those early materials—have the potential to go much faster, especially if you can do it at the scale that we've done it, especially if you can do it at the low capital infusions that we've been able to do. We have not raised a lot of money at Leash, and we've screened an enormous amount. And then I think, getting even stepping back, one of the reasons that I brought up this language model stuff is because we are starting to wonder if it would enable a much larger scope of capabilities than just identifying novel chemical material. Like if we get really good at chemical reasoning, then we can get really good at lots of different industries and their applications without having to physically go and screen in all those different domains.

consensus.en: DNA-encoded libraries enable scalable measurement of small molecule binding.
consensus.zh: DNA编码库能够大规模测量小分子结合。

consensus.en: Public data is contaminated by sociological fingerprints, not ground truth.
consensus.zh: 公共数据被社会学指纹污染，而非真实信号。

consensus.en: Scaling data collection across proteins and chemicals is key to progress.
consensus.zh: 跨蛋白质和化学品的规模化数据收集是进步的关键。

consensus.en: Models must be evaluated on out-of-distribution data to avoid memorization.
consensus.zh: 模型必须在分布外数据上评估以避免记忆。

consensus.en: Language models with reinforcement learning can reason about chemistry.
consensus.zh: 语言模型结合强化学习可以推理化学。

consensus.en: Activity cliffs and mutations teach models causal relationships.
consensus.zh: 活性悬崖和突变教会模型因果关系。

contrarian.en: Models trained on public data learn sociology, not physics.
contrarian.zh: 在公共数据上训练的模型学习社会学，而非物理。

contrarian.en: Molecular weight predicts binding due to data bias, not chemistry.
contrarian.zh: 分子量预测结合是由于数据偏差，而非化学。

contrarian.en: Simple SMILES representations outperform complex 3D models.
contrarian.zh: 简单的SMILES表示优于复杂的3D模型。

contrarian.en: Attention maps reveal models memorize protein nicknames, not pockets.
contrarian.zh: 注意力图揭示模型记忆蛋白质昵称，而非口袋。

contrarian.en: Reinforcement learning with language models resists memorization better.
contrarian.zh: 语言模型结合强化学习更能抵抗记忆。

contrarian.en: Data collection scale matters more than model architecture sophistication.
contrarian.zh: 数据收集规模比模型架构复杂性更重要。
